expected_evidence: geological: cosmogenic isotope spikes (¹⁰Be, ³⁶Cl) in Greenland ice cores (GISP2/GRIP/NGRIP) coincident with ~10,900–10,800 BCE, indicative of a sudden ionizing-radiation flux
geological: nitrate/ammonium concentration anomalies in ice layers consistent with ozone-layer disruption from gamma-ray ionization
astronomical (proxy): radiocarbon (¹⁴C) production spikes in contemporaneous tree-ring or other cosmogenic-nuclide archives (a 'Miyake-type' event) matching the ice-core signal
material: sedimentary/geomorphological evidence of the meltwater pulse itself (proglacial lake drainage channels, outwash deposits, e.g. Lake Agassiz spillway sediments) dated to the same interval
material: fine annual ice-layer stratigraphy showing an abrupt onset of Younger Dryas cooling (dust, δ18O shift) temporally correlated with the isotope anomaly
genetic: megafaunal or human population bottleneck signatures dated near onset, offered as secondary/circumstantial support
model-prior: theoretical atmospheric-chemistry modeling linking a gamma-ray ionization event to ozone depletion and abrupt cooling (not itself physical evidence, low-tier)
response.rationale: The hypothesis links three components: (1) a meltwater pulse, (2) Younger Dryas onset cooling, and (3) a proposed gamma-ray-ionization mechanism, all placed at the Greenland ice sheet during 11,000–10,001 BCE — squarely the Younger Dryas period. Critically, the hypothesis's own action field is 'inconclusive', signaling that even the hypothesis engine does not assert this connection is established; it is presented as an open, testable proposition rather than a confirmed causal claim. This matches the real-world scientific status of such ideas (e.g., proposed links between cosmogenic-isotope spikes, a possible nearby transient radiation event or solar proton event, and Younger Dryas onset) — recalled here only as model-prior, since I have no verified source text confirming specifics of this exact 'gamma-ray-ionization' claim. If broadly true, the expected evidence would be almost entirely physical/proxy in nature: ice-core cosmogenic isotopes, nitrate/ozone-depletion chemistry, radiocarbon spikes, and meltwater-pulse sedimentology — no textual, linguistic, or iconographic evidence could exist, since this predates writing and settled iconography by millennia (textual detectability = 0.0, linguistic = 0.05, iconographic = 0.10). Fortunately, the hypothesis's *placement itself* — Greenland ice sheet — is precisely the archive type with the highest detectability scores in this period: astronomical/cosmogenic-proxy evidence (0.70) and geological ice-core stratigraphy (0.65) are both well above average, because Greenland ice cores are continuously laminated, well-dated, and specifically preserve isotopic and chemical signals of exactly this kind. Material evidence for the meltwater pulse (glacial lake drainage geomorphology) is moderately detectable (0.35), and genetic evidence weaker (0.30) and only indirectly relevant. Given this, absence of confirmed causal attribution is not strong evidence the mechanism did not occur — ice cores could preserve an isotope spike coincident with the cooling onset, yet whether it stems specifically from a gamma-ray ionization event versus solar activity, volcanism, or measurement noise is inherently hard to disentangle from proxy signals alone. This ambiguity is consistent with the hypothesis's own 'inconclusive' action label. Weighting toward the two strongest applicable channels (geological, astronomical-proxy) while discounting weaker material/genetic support and zeroing out textual/linguistic, a detectability adjustment of ~0.58 seems appropriate: the physical archive (Greenland ice) is unusually favorable for preserving relevant chemical/isotopic evidence, but a low-to-moderate score reflects that attribution to a specific ionizing mechanism (vs. alternative causes) remains scientifically ambiguous and not a matter of preservation failure.
